utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, will you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, case number IT-98-32/I-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We are here for a Rule 11 bis. I'd like to have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. Susan Somers for the Prosecution, accompanied to my right by Mr. Aleksandar Kontic, to his right Ms. Carmela Javier, case manager, and behind me Mr. Greg Bodulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. For the Defence. First the Defence of Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Djuro Cepic, Defence counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic. On my left-hand side is Mr. Jens Dieckmann, as a co-counsel on Defence team, and also appearing with us is Mr. Erez Zaionce, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. For the Defence of Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, members of the Prosecution, guests from the states of Serbia, Bosnia, and Argentina. My name is Alan Yatvin and I represent the accused, Mr. Milan Lukic. Check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I have the appearances for Argentina. Could you please introduce yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was interrupted by my counsellor. Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am the Ambassador of Argentina, Santos Goni, and I am accompanied by a counsellor to my embassy, Silvia Raiola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have representatives of Serbia as well. Could they introduce themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, my name is Sasa Obradovic. I am the first ambassador of the embassy, and with me I have Dusan Knezevic who is the deputy prosecutor for war crimes of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Obradovic. We have been in contact with the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could I have the appearances from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To my left, Ms. Biljana Potparic, deputy registrar of the office of the registrar of the divisions 1 and 2 of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mr. Mirsad Strika of the prosecutor's office of the Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mr. Emir Neradin, and Ms. Metjir Blaud [phoen] from the office of the registrar for departments 1 and 2 of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and Mr. Toby Cadman, prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, of course, myself, Miljana Popadic from the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Popadic. Then, Mr. Sredoje Lukic, the parties have introduced themselves. Were you able to hear them in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED SREDOJE LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same question for you, Mr. Milan Lukic. THE ACCUSED MILAN LUKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Please be seated. We have informed the parties about the order of this meeting. The Chamber stresses again that we'd like to hear any addition to what's already on paper. There's no need to repeat whatever you've written down already. I'd like to give first an opportunity to the Prosecution to address the Chamber. Fifteen minutes are available, and I'll be very strict on time. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. First of all, the Prosecution would like to vociferously express its objection to Serbia's intervention at this time. It was not part of the designation by the Prosecution or by the Trial Referral Bench proprio motu, as is required by the Rule. We recognise the Chamber did request the presence but we have not had an opportunity formally to object to the actual interjection, given the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, this is in line with earlier case law of this Referral Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We stand firmly on our submissions. The Prosecution, because it was not asked to comment on any aspect of the issues concerning Argentina's presence, has reserved any comment, and if the Chamber would like to hear from us on our view, we would offer it. But because it was not an official written request, we have simply hesitated. Above and beyond, we deem that this case is fully appropriate for referral as for both accused. The additional submissions that have come in have not persuaded us to advance any further argument above and beyond what was laid out in our response to the submissions, in your order of 30 June. And with the Chamber's permission, if we may be permitted to listen to any further argument that might require comment and return or seek audience if there is something additional after having heard, because I don't know what else might be raised by our colleagues and by our learned and esteemed guests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, to answer your questions and also to inform the parties, whatever time is saved in, I would say, the first round, - you had 50 minutes available, you've used 3 until now - that time is, if not entirely but at least is to some extent available for you to respond to others; and this is true for the other parties as well, the shorter you are in the first round. But don't start saying, all of you, that you have nothing to add, because then we're already in the second round. But you'll have an opportunity to respond if any other issue is raised and if you have not yet addressed that matter in your written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to give an opportunity to the representatives of Argentina to address the specific issue raised. As you may be aware of, the Referral Bench has formulated a provisional view on what the meaning is of the decision of the Argentinian court, and that is the specific reason, very specific reason why we invite you to come. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please activate your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: May I sit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: I will read in Spanish the opinion of the Argentine government regarding the point before the Bench today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your Excellency, at this moment we do not receive the translation. What channel should we choose to receive English translation on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to start again and to read not too quickly because otherwise the interpreters might have difficulties in following your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: The full text has been handed to the Registrar in advance and is therefore available to the Court. [Interpretation] "In keeping with the request made by the Referral Bench, an order dated 30th June this year, the opinion of the Argentinian government is given as regards the relationship between the sentence handed down on the 10th of January 2006 by the national federal court number 8 of Argentina, whereby Mr. Lukic was surrendered to the ICTY, and Rule 11 bis on referral of the indictment to another court, under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. "On this point, let me point out clearly that the Argentinian court decided, with the consent given by the defendant, to accede to the request for transfer and surrender submitted by ICTY for the accused to be tried at the seat of the Tribunal, it being clear that he could not be referred to another place in order to be charged, prosecuted or harassed without the prior authorisation of the Argentinian state. "Likewise, the Argentinian court decided to accede and, given the request by the Government of Serbia and Montenegro, and acceded therefore to the -- having Mr. Milan Lukic extradited, it being clear, obviously, that the full process be complied with as requested by the ICTY." As a consequence of which, on the 21st of February, this year, Milan Lukic was surrendered to ICTY for him to be tried by this Tribunal and afterwards by the judicial authorities of Serbia. This is why a verbal note of the Tribunal was submitted to the Argentinian embassy in The Hague, whereby the Tribunal thanked the Argentinian authorities for all the assistance given. Thereafter, the Tribunal made it clear that all the conditions were met in order to renew procedure in keeping with Rule 11 bis, under which the Prosecutor asked for the case against Mr. Lukic to be referred to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for it to be tried by the corresponding court in that state in keeping with Resolutions 1534/04 and 1503/03 of the United Nations Security Council. The Referral Bench considered, as stated in order dated 30th June 2006, that, in keeping with the previous consideration carried out by Argentina, this dissension -- Argentina's decision would have a Tribunal for Milan Lukic, at the seat of the Tribunal for the crimes referred to in the official indictment, or that the Tribunal may fully exert its powers in keeping with the Statute of the Tribunal, Rule 11 bis, and resolutions 1534 and 1503 of the Security Council of the United Nations to refer Milan Lukic and for him to be tried by a competent authority but not without the prior authorisation given by the Argentinian state. And this is why the ICTY invited the embassy of the Argentinian Republic to submit its opinion on the relationship between the sentence of the Argentinian Tribunal and the referral procedures of ICTY under Rule 11 bis, specifically ICTY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down. It's a common experience that, when reading, speed goes up and the interpreters ask you to slow down. Please proceed. I have on my screen -- perhaps you could resume there where you said "This is why we asked" ... Could you resume there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Consequently, the Tribunal invited the embassy of the Argentinian Republic to submit its opinion on the relationship between the sentence handed down by the Argentinian court and the referral procedures of the International Criminal Tribunal in keeping with Rule 11 bis. Specifically, ICTY invited the Argentinian government to attend the hearing to be held on the 15th of September and to show whether it shares the provisional opinion mentioned in the previous paragraph as regards the effects of the Argentinian decision. If one reads carefully the order given by the Referral Bench on the 30th of June, it is clear that when you analyse the Argentinian sentence, in fact, the Tribunal sees two possibilities. The first such possibility: The sentence handed down by the Argentinian court makes it clear that Milan Lukic must be tried only by the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia, it being clear that the case can not be referred to another Tribunal. And the second possibility is that ICTY may invoke Rule 11 bis, referring thereby the case to a competent national Tribunal in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although previously authorisation must be sought from the Argentinian state. In principle, it should be pointed out that the Argentinian decision enabled the transfer and surrender of Lukic to the ICTY for him to be tried there for the crimes mentioned in the formal indictment, in the official indictment. In the order of transfer and surrender given by the Court, there was absolutely no mention of the motion submitted by the Prosecution to refer the case to a competent national authority under Rule 11 bis. In other words, in the ICTY order, there was no warning given to the Argentinian Republic as to the possible transfer of the case to a tribunal of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Such a possibility arises after Lukic was surrendered, when the Tribunal informed that the Prosecution gave notification as to the fulfilment of the conditions, that is to say, the presence of the accused before the Tribunal, in order to settle the transfer motion that had been presented, in order to reach a decision on this motion. Likewise, we should keep in mind that whilst Lukic was detained in Buenos Aries to be transferred to The Hague, the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not ask for extradition, nor did it show any interest whatsoever in his detention for him to be extradited. Moreover, according to the informal information that we have received through the Interpol department of the federal police of Argentina, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not issued an order of international capture against Mr. Lukic. On the contrary, such an interest had indeed been made clear by the Government of Serbia. The Serbian embassy did ask for the extradition of Mr. Lukic, which afterwards was acceded to, even though surrender to this country was conditioned to the ICTY process being totally complied with first, by virtue of which -- this is a new paragraph. By virtue of the aforesaid, it can be stated without any doubt that the intention and interest of the Argentinian authorities will be fulfilled by the Security Council, giving the widest possible cooperation to the ICTY for the fulfilment of its lofty goals. And recognising the supremacy of the jurisdiction of this Tribunal faced with the request presented by Serbia. This is the reason why Lukic was surrendered to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and his extradition was made conditional on the decision taken by ICTY. Consequently, and as regards the interpretation of the Argentinian sentence, without prejudice to the fact that our authorities had received no previous warning as regards the transfer motion that had been presented so as to transfer the case to the Bosnia-Herzegovina case -- motion that had been presented by the Prosecution, in no way can this sentence be interpreted as undermining the exercise of the powers of transfer of this Tribunal. All the more so, as such powers, the possibility therefore of transferring a case to a competent national authority is indeed contemplated within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and since the authorities of the Republic of Argentina have clearly shown full cooperation from the very beginning of this case. It is thus to be noted, furthermore, that the procedure -- that the procedure for re-extraditing is provided for in domestic legislation in Argentina. Law 24.767, law 24767, lays down in Article 18 that a person extradited from the Republic of Argentina cannot be - cannot be - re-extradited to another state without the prior authorisation granted by Argentina, unless the person extradited should -- unless the person extradited should freely and expressly forego such possibility. The procedure to obtain such an authorisation is laid down in Article 54 of the law I have just mentioned. In consideration wherof, and bearing in mind the rules applicable both within ICTY and within Argentinian legislation, as well as the sentence handed down by Argentinian justice and the renewed willingness to cooperate shown by this Republic with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the Government of the Argentinian Republic would like to see the case of Lukic tried by the Tribunal at its seat, in keeping with the Argentinian decision. And without prejudice to this, should there be an order to transfer the trial to a national competent court, in keeping with Rule 11 bis, the necessary authorisation should be sought from the Argentinian state, in keeping with the procedure that has been laid down to that effect in Argentinian legislation, in the light of the last part of the 10th, considering of the order of the 30th of June ordered by the Referral Bench; that is to say, the Tribunal may exert its powers to transfer Milan Lukic, for him to be tried by a competent national tribunal, but such transfer should not take place without prior authorisation from the Argentinian state. Thank you very much, indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the translator, the last paragraph is connected to the previous one. In fact, there should be a comma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to give an opportunity to the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina to address the Court on any matter which is not yet part of their written submissions. Ms. Popadic, may I invite you to address the Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to point out that the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina abide by all the arguments they have provided and all the written responses regarding this particular case, as well as all the oral and written submissions of the relevant institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided in other cases which may be of assistance to the Chamber in issuing the proper decision, bearing in mind the positive experiences in connection with the cases referred up to now to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as the Stankovic, Jankovic, and Meakic at our cases, and the new cases which are expected to be referred soon, as well as the cases initiated by the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are being conducted without impediment, we believe that the judicial system of Bosnia-Herzegovina is fully ready to take over this case. I also wish to point out that the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, over the previous several months, have undertaken the necessary steps to ensure the necessary funds in order to provide for the unhindered operation of the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the forthcoming period. Therefore, I wish to stress that Bosnia-Herzegovina is fully prepared to take the case of Milan and Sredoje Lukic for further proceedings. And we are willing to answer any questions put by the Chamber or other interested parties. I therefore undertake to submit a written response of any question that may be put to us by the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Popadic. Next submission on the agenda is by the representative of Serbia. Mr. Obradovic, may I invite you to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me to thank you, first of all, for inviting us to attend this hearing, for enabling us to present the views of our government in relation to the referral of the case against Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic to domestic judiciary. In that respect, we ask that the written submission submitted on behalf of the Government of Serbia, on the 4th of September, by Mr. Rasim Lajic, the president of the National Council for Cooperation with the ICTY be treated by you as an initiative, proprio motu, on behalf of Serbia for referring this case to Serbia in accordance with Rule 11 bis (B). Given your order on scheduling this hearing, I will not be repeating any assurances of goodwill of our country and government to take over this case and thus contribute to the administration of justice and rule of law in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. This is something that the highest representatives of our government spoke already about to you in other cases. Instead, I will give you some reasons that would justify the referral of this case to the Serbian judiciary. By doing so, I wish to emphasise that Mr. Knezevic, the deputy prosecutor, and I will be speaking today about the alleged crimes and guilt of the accused only within the framework of this very special procedure and based on the facts contained in the indictment, not wishing to bring into question the presumption of innocence of the two accused, which represents one of the fundamental legal principles of the criminal procedure in Serbia. We already spoke to you in our written submission about the fact that there were two trials against Milan Lukic held before the war crimes chamber of the district court in Belgrade. He was charged by the indictment of the ICTY OTP in one case and he was also convicted in Belgrade in a case where the victims were Muslims from Serbia and Montenegro, who were kidnapped from a bus and from a train. This is why we believe that the principle of good administration of justice makes it mandatory for us to ensure that all of the cases for which Milan Lukic is charged be tried simultaneously before one court. This is simultaneously in the interests of the accused but also in the interest of victims and witnesses. This is the interest of judicial economy. We unfortunately have to state that this is an interest not recognised by the Prosecution of this Tribunal in their submissions. The same principle, known as good administration of justice, makes it mandatory that the co-accused Sredoje Lukic also be tried simultaneously by this same court. By conducting a single trial before the war crimes chamber of the district court in Belgrade, there would undoubtedly be a step towards contributing to the further good development of cooperation between the judiciary of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And so far this contribution has been assessed as very successful by Mrs. Del Ponte. She said so when addressing the permanent council of the OSCE recently in Vienna. It seems that the war crimes court in Bosnia-Herzegovina was currently encountering serious financial difficulties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you to slow down. It's common experience that reading always goes quicker than formulating your words not from paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I will try. I will try, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Especially towards the final comments in the submission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we find some indication that the judiciary of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not able to ensure efficient proceedings in this case. We believe that the referral of this case to Serbia would, in no way, violate the decision of the Argentine court in relation to the accused Milan Lukic. Furthermore, I wish to inform you about the interest of the Government of Serbia for holding this trial in our country. It is certain that the position and international reputation of the war crimes prosecutor as well as the war crimes chamber of the Republic of Serbia would be strengthened by conducting proper proceedings in such cases, which is clearly in the interests of our country. On the other hand, the citizens of Serbia would be best informed and would best face the terrible crimes committed during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina if the trial were to be held in their presence, in their country. Any judgement against Serbs for crimes committed against members of other ethnic groups and religions would be best accepted if it were pronounced by a local domestic court. On the other hand, there is no concern that the court, who in absentia had already convicted Milan Lukic to a 20-year sentence, would all of a sudden decide to spare him in this case. The results received so far by the war crimes prosecutor and the war crimes chamber in Belgrade have been uniformly viewed as very successful. There is a European Union document that states that the Ovcara case held in Belgrade should be used as a model for all other countries in the region as to how to conduct war crimes trials. The cooperation between the Belgrade prosecutor and the Tribunal is excellent. There is no reason for this Chamber, Your Honours, to believe that it is not justified to show faith in the Serbian judiciary by referring this case to Serbia, which hasn't been the case so far. The OTP seems to give priority to the criteria of the place where the crimes were committed, and it is undoubtedly in the interest of the victims and their families. But, however, this criteria was limited to the state level. These crimes were committed neither in Sarajevo, nor in Belgrade, but rather in a border region of Visegrad. Then why should the trial be held in Sarajevo and not in Belgrade? The Prosecution of this Tribunal did something quite the opposite in the case of crimes committed in the vicinity of Zvornik, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The case was referred to Serbia in the stage of investigation, and this trial is now in progress successfully before the war crimes chamber of the district court in Belgrade. In relation to all other matters, we stand by the arguments contained in our written submissions, although I do have to point out that paragraph 7 found its way into this written submission by means of an obvious bureaucratic mistake. Therefore, I urge you to ignore this paragraph, and I apologise for this. My distinguished colleague, Mr. Knezevic, will say a few words about the possibility to have this case tried before a court in Serbia. Since we got involved in this procedure at quite a late stage, we had no opportunity to answer the questions that were addressed by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, I ask you to yield the floor to Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Knezevic, before I give you an opportunity to add something to what has been said already by Mr. Obradovic, as I said before, 15 minutes was the time limit. I'm a bit concerned that what you might want to bring to our attention might not fit well within the minutes that remain, and to inform you that would be five minutes, only. Could you do it in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, learned friends, ladies and gentlemen. I know that my time is limited to five minutes. I will do my best to respond to the issues raised here within that time. The 11 bis Rule of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in 11 bis (A), under (iii), provides for the possibility of referring the case to a country having jurisdiction and being willing and adequately prepared to accept such a case. The law on the organisation and competence of state organs against perpetrators of war crimes of the Republic of Serbia of 2003, which was amended in 2004, establishes the competence of the state organs of Serbia to try all cases of war crimes committed on the territory of the former SFRY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, may I just interrupt you? Isn't it true that in the submissions, that it's already set out that Serbia can exercise jurisdiction and even allows the prosecution of crimes committed by citizens of Serbia, wherever committed. So the jurisdiction aspect seems to be covered by the written submissions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you have said, Your Honours. I won't repeat myself. But this law provides for the possibility of trying all cases of war crimes, regardless of the nationality of the perpetrator and the victim. I only wish to add to what our Ambassador has said, is that the willingness of our state to try this case is evident from the fact that we have already initiated proceedings and that there is a sentence against Milan Lukic. He has been sentenced to 20 years in prison for war crimes. We ask the State of Argentina to extradite Milan Lukic to us, or to refer him to us for trial. And I wish to add again - it's very difficult to raise all the important issues in five minutes - but the issue of territorial jurisdiction mentioned in point 2, we are talking about a small area of land, about 7 kilometres wide, between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. I have to point out that there is a law on the protection of participants in criminal proceedings of January 2006, the 1st of January, 2006, and I think it's important to add that everything charged against Sredoje Lukic in the indictment can be tried without any obstacles in the State of Serbia. And I also wish to add that a unified proceeding could be instituted in our country and carried through for all the crimes he is charged with. We also have an agreement on cooperation with Bosnia and Herzegovina, signed by the war crimes prosecutor in Belgrade and the Sarajevo -- his counter-part in Sarajevo. The case of Dvornik was referred to our country, and all the witnesses from Bosnia-Herzegovina travelled to Belgrade without any hinderance and testified with no obstacle, and all this shows that the agreement is functioning well. If I can answer any questions of yours, I will be very happy to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Knezevic. On the agenda next is submissions, oral submissions, by the Defence, and counsel are invited to divide the time in good cooperation. Were you able to do so? Mr. Yatvin.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we reached a Solomonic decision and split it in half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you also decide who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I drew the short straw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Yatvin, then, you have got 20 out of these 40 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And it is likewise my intention to ask the Bench to reserve part of that time, because I'm assuming that the Prosecution will have argument on the new material that's been here today, and I'd like to be able to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was already our ruling. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Just when it seemed there was nothing new in the universe of 11 bis, here we are. I -- in light of the submissions by the Republic of Argentina and their Ambassador today, I think I should probably start with that issue. I ask the Court to consider the fact of how we got here, how Mr. Lukic comes to be in this room. He was taken into custody in Argentina, and the Federal Court of Argentina considered the request of the Tribunal to transfer him, and the Republic of Argentina is, of course, a member of the United Nations, and the Statute of the Tribunal, which is the hand of the United Nations, compels all member nations to cooperate with the transfer request to the Tribunal. And that's how he comes to be here. But the next step that the Prosecutor asks this Bench to take is not from the Statute of the Tribunal, and it's not necessarily from the Security Council either, because in order to make this next step, this Bench must say that the sovereign nation of Argentina does not have a right to control its extradition process. And I submit that this Court would be serving as a mere conduit for the nation of Bosnia-Herzegovina which did not see fit to make a request of Argentina to transfer. Now, I know that there have been other cases where this Court has ruled that the so-called u-turn or re-transfer is not barred by the nation surrendering the accused to the Tribunal, but in all those cases, the argument was made by operation of law, because the surrendering nation has this statute on its books, therefore you should not transfer. What makes this situation unique is that the Federal Court of Argentina considered the question, considered an application from Bosnia, considered the transfer to this Court, and made a specific ruling that, complying with our obligation, we will surrender Mr. Lukic to the Tribunal and we contemplate a trial before that Tribunal; but we are not giving up our rights to control transferring to somewhere else. Now, of course, the Tribunal has a Rule of Procedure, 11 bis, which authorises that transfer, but the problem this Bench must wrestle with is whether the judge-made rule of 11 bis, unlike the Statute of the Tribunal, trumps the rights and the imperatives of the sovereign nation of Argentina, and I would submit it does not. I will move on from the issue of Argentina. As the Court has pointed out, we have briefed this rather thoroughly in at least two sets of submissions, and I don't want to go back chapter and verse. But I feel the need to comment on something that Ms. Somers opened with this afternoon. She stated: We stand firmly on our submissions. That's really the point I tried to make in my submissions, that Prosecutor does not stand firmly on their submissions. What submissions did she stand up firmly on today? Her 11 bis Motion, where they characterised Mr. Lukic as the most individually responsible for killings of anyone in the conflict and the most responsible for conduct throughout the territory at that time of Bosnia and Herzegovina? No. They've withdrawn that. So that admission, they do not stand on. Do they stand on what they said before a member of this Bench sitting at the Trial Chamber -- in the Trial Chamber in the Popovic case in their opening argument? No, they don't stand on that. They want this Court to artificially narrow itself to solely the indictment for deciding role and -- I mean offence -- gravity of offence and role in the commission of that offence. I understand the genesis of the Rule. Obviously this Court is the genesis of that Rule. You've sat on all those arguments. You've made all those decisions that compromise -- comprise what we consider is the law here today. But I submit that the application of that Rule which this Court made in good faith at the beginning is no longer logical in this case; that stare decisis, the rule of precedent is important but it is not irrevocable. In this case you have the situation where the Prosecutor herself has placed information before this Tribunal and that information should not be disregarded in deciding the role of Mr. -- the gravity of the offences and the role of Mr. Lukic in the conflict. And, again, he's presumed innocent. I'm only discussing the allegations. There's obviously no admission of any liability. But it's very important that you look to the language of the President of the Security Counsel which is referenced in the Security Council resolutions which are referenced in Rule 11 bis, which is not limiting to the specific conduct charge, but it talks about the role of the persons in the area under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, in the conflict. As I've argued, and I won't go through it again in great detail, that even if you're considering only the crimes charged in this indictment, which was in fact tailored during the time of the Rule 11 bis proceeding itself, you still have to look at Mr. Lukic's alleged role in the conflict, in the broader conflict, not only in the crime charged. Under those circumstances, he, the crimes, and the role in those crimes are not appropriate for referral. I refer the Court to the arguments made by the Government of Serbia that there are reasons of judicial economy and of unity in proceedings that the case should be referred to Serbia, which is within this Court's powers. And I'm going to reserve the rest of my time, if I may, and I'm hopeful that the Court will assist me to assist it by asking some questions at the appropriate time, because I'm sure there are some, and I'd like to be able to respond to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Yatvin. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend, Mr. Jens Dieckmann will raise our altitude and -- on behalf of our Defence team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dieckmann, you are invited to make your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Jens Dieckmann, I'm attorney at law from Germany, and I represent the accused, Mr. Lukic, as co-counsel in this procedure. In a statement for the Defence, I would like to focus on the question of their trial and the applicable law, not only repeating and referring to the submissions we've have presented, but going in detail to some case law we prepared, some case law and practice. And we have looked how this legal frame work is working in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are well aware of the frame and the formal decisions of the Referral Bench, for example, the decision on the referral in the case from 8 July 2005, as the Referral Bench described its jurisdiction regarding the questions of applicable law as follows. "The Referral Bench stresses that it is not the competent authority to decide in any binding way which law is to be applied in this case if it is referred to Bosnia. It is a matter which would be in the competence of the state court of Bosnia if referral is ordered. The Bench must be satisfied, however, that if the case against either or both accused were to be referred, there would exist in Bosnia an adequate legal framework." The Defence respectfully submits that this Referral Bench must base its decision today on the actual viable facts and circumstances as they currently exist. To be adequately prepared is not only a question of the legal frame work, but the fair trial principle and every question related to this has to do with court practice. The Referral Bench has expressed in several decisions that trusts that the state court of Bosnia will exercise its power with competent under the rule of law in the system of public international law and in a way compatible with the principles of fair trial. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, if you would allow me to intervene for one second. The quote you started with, clearly in the case law of this Referral Bench, relates to the application of substantive law and not -- is not about procedural law, not about fairness. It seems to me that you're starting with a consideration on substantive law and then give it a follow-up in terms of procedural law, whereas, as far as I'm concerned, but my learned colleagues will certainly intervene when I'm wrong in understanding our own decisions, that the procedural law is dealt with in our parts of our decisions. Please proceed, and keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence refers to three decisions of the war crime chamber of the state court of Bosnia in order to show that the war crime chamber is up to now not able to find the applicable law under the rule of law in a fair trial procedure. We have to state a relevant lack of competence in the application of the basic rules of public international law, causing dramatic consequences for the accused. The first decision we want to refer to is a decision, 1st July, 2005, of the war crime chamber of the state court of Bosnia, sentencing Mr. Abulahim Maktuf [phoen] to imprisonment. The appeal has been dismissed on the 4th of the April, 2006. This is not a referral case. But he was found guilty as an accessory in the taking of the three Croat civilians as hostages by the Mujahedin unit in Travnik in 1993. The legal position of the Defence in this case has been that Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia should be applied, given that, after the abolition of capital punishment, the sanction referred to in Article 142 of the Criminal Code of former Yugoslavia is a more lenient sanction compared to the criminal sanction stipulated in Article 173(1) of the Criminal Code of Bosnia. And that it is a legal principle which includes mandatory application of the Criminal Code. The war crime chamber found that such argument is not found, and that in the concrete case, the provision referred to in Article 173(1) of the Bosnian Criminal Code has to be applied. The arguments of the war crime chamber has been the following: First, to start with Article 3 of the Bosnian Criminal Code. It stipulates the principle of legality, that is said the verdict can only be founded on the principle which existed at the time when the incriminated act or failure to act happened. This is a principle ruling nullum crimen sine lege. In Article 4 of the Bosnian Criminal Code, it stipulates that the law which was in effect at the time when the criminal offence was perpetrated should apply to the perpetrator of the criminal offence and, Article 4(2), if the law has been amended on one or more occasions, the law that is the more lenient law to be perpetrator shall be applied. This is the lex mitior principle in the Bosnian Criminal Code. In Article 4(a) of the Bosnian Criminal Code, amended in the year of 2004, it regulates that Article 3 and 4 should not prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal offence according to the general principle of international law. The war crime chamber holds the view that this Article 4(a) adopted completely the provision of Article 7(2) on the European Convention on Human Rights, this providing for exceptional departure from application of the principle referred to in Article 4 in the criminal code of Bosnia, as well as for mandatory application of a more lenient law in the proceedings representing criminal offences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: -- because it's exactly the offence which includes violation of international law. Therefore, this is the conclusion of the war crime chamber: Article 4(a) of the Criminal Code is applied to all criminal offences in war crime cases. The second decision of the war crime chamber we are referring to is the case of Mr. Nedzo Samardzic. He was sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment under Article 172 by the judgement of 7 April 2006. First of all, the war crime chamber repeats exactly the same aforementioned arguments of the Maktuf case complemented by the following points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've resumed but the speed is still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The war crime chamber states in addition, I may quote: "In relation to this, the Court points out that the crimes laid down in the indictment at the time relevant to the indictment constitutes crime under international customary law. International customary law is part of the general principles of international law as stipulated in Article 4(a) of the Bosnian Criminal Code." And then the war crime chamber gives a short list of some examples why they have the opinion that this is customary international law. They just give a list of the report of Secretary General of the United Nations, international law commissions draft, and his quotation from international court, ICTR, in Arusha. No comment, no explanation, no discussion. And at least the war crime chamber has the opinion that the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights stresses the applicability of the provision of Article 7(2) in the judgement of 4th May 2000 in the case Naletilic against Croatia in their point. These two above-mentioned decisions of the war crime chamber contain view to the point of the Defence, several substantial legal errors which consequently lead to unlawful and an absolute exclusion of the lex mitior principle in war crime cases at the war crime chamber in Bosnia. The first point: Article 4(a), the Bosnian Criminal Code, is in fact not identical with Article 7(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The war crime chamber ignores the evident difference between general principles of international law - this is the reading in Article 4A of the Bosnian Criminal Code - and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations. This is a reading of Article 7(2) on the European Convention on Human Rights. The words from Article 7(2) have been taken from Article 38(1)(c) from the Statute of the International Court of Justice. This is undisputed in opinio juris and this is undisputed in court decisions. The second point is more dramatic. The second point is that the understanding of Article 7(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights is wrong. This rule is a subsidiary rule. This can only be applied if there is a loophole or gap to take this. This comes therefrom, of course, Article 7(2) transfers the Article 38 reading of the International Court of Justice statute. As we can read in the commentary for the ICJ statute of appellant, I may quote: "Yet they, the principles, are subsidiary in the sense that the Court will usually only resort to them for filling a gap in the treaty or customary rule available to settle a particular dispute, and what is even more apparent will decline to invoke them when such other rule exist." In consequence, only in the time the criminal acts have taken place, these acts did not constitute crimes under national laws, then Article 7(2) is applicable. Here the alleged crimes of the accused has been evidently covered by Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the former Yugoslavia at the time the criminal acts allegedly should have been committed. Therefore, there is no legal gap, no loophole justifying the application of Article 7(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights, and therefore there is no justification for a complete exclusion of Article 4(2) of the Bosnian Criminal Code, it means of the lex mitior principle. Therefore, in consequence of Article 2, paragraph 2, of the constitution of Bosnia which states that the European Convention on Human Rights always overrules contradictory national law. Article 4(A) of the Bosnian Criminal Code cannot allow the exclusion of Article 4(2). Article 7(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights forbids the exclusion of the lex mitior principle if there is, as here, no case of subsidiarity given. The third decision we refer to is a judgement from 26 May 2006 in the Panovic case who was sentenced to long-term imprisonment for 20 years. This decision was only six weeks after the last decision of Mr. Omadovic. In this judgement, the war crime chamber, again, repeated the same argument from Article 3, Article 4 for (A), and Article 7(2) for the European Convention on Human Rights. But then without any explanation, any justification, any discussion of their former position, the court states now, six weeks later: "Article 4(A) of the Bosnian Criminal Code speaks of general principles of international law. As neither international law nor the European Convention on Human Rights are familiar with the identical term, this term actually represents a combination of principles of international law and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations." This understanding is due to the position of the Defence, again, wrong. But principles of general -- general principles of international law are definitely not the combination of something. They are part of customary international law. We don't know if the war crime chamber tries to tell us that the legislature of Bosnia is creating new sources of public international law in their national criminal law. We do not understand this reading. In the following of this decision, the war crime chamber, in June 2006, repeats again the wrong definition of Article 7(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights. They, again, misinterpret the subsidiary nature of this norm. Our position that Article 7(2) is only a subsidiary norm is supported in fact by the reading and by the decisions of the European Convention on Human Rights in Strasbourg, and we want to quote the single and the most important decision. This is the decision of the 22nd March 2001. It was the decision against Krens, Kursla [phoen], and Strelitz, the former leaders of the east German -- eastern German republic, and in this decision, the European court in Strasbourg has said that the crimes has been correctly decided by the national criminal courts under the national Criminal Code under force at the time of the commitment. We do not understand how the Bosnian government and the war crime chamber repeat frequent times that the case of Naletilic against Croatia should be a reference for the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, you would not mind if I draw your attention to the fact that you are now speaking for 15 minutes. Could you please try to sum up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So at least, Your Honour, I think -- we think that here the argumentation of the war crime chamber based on a wrong understanding of the basic rules of public international law, a wrong understanding of the human rights convention on human rights which leads to a permanent consequent exclusion of the principle of lex mitior. This court has expressed trust that this war crime chamber is able to find applicable law under the rule of law in a fair trial. The court decisions we have presented here think -- could have illustrated that there is a great irritation and a lack of competence, and we are not sure that this is acceptable here for the accused we are defending. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: One short correction, in the transcript, page 30, line 16, my learned friend said lex mitior and I see something different is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes the transcript will be corrected overnight and -- well, of course, since we're speaking some Latin now, it's not always easy and that the transcribers do an excellent job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I give the opportunity to use the remainder of the time for the parties, I would like to take the opportunity and give the opportunity to the Judges, to the Bench, to put additional questions to the parties and the representatives of states present today. Yes. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was triggered by Mr. Yatvin. My question is to Ms. Somers, to the Prosecution. It is obvious that there are substantial differences between the amended indictment of July -- 12th of July, 2001, and the currently operative indictment, the second amended indictment of November 2005. The previous indictment, at paragraph 28, charges both the accused, along with Mitar Vasiljevic, with all the forms of responsibility under Article 7(2). It also alleges that the three accused acted in concert with one another in the realisation of the charged crimes which the Prosecution argued in the Vasiljevic case was meant to include participation in a joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Vasiljevic on the basis of joint criminal enterprise in its November 2002 judgement, holding that his participation in this joint criminal enterprise with Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. However, in the current indictment, by contrast, all the forms of responsibility have been removed, except physical perpetration and aiding and abetting. The crime base allegations have also been cut down to allege a more confined geographic area. This is, indeed, a very curious and rare type of amendment I know. Instead of adding charges against the accused, the Prosecution took them away. What concerns me about this is that the motion to amend the previous indictment was submitted on 17th November, 2005, subsequent to the referral request which took place on 1st of February last year, and after the Stankovic decision in May. So my question to you is this: Was the purpose behind this amendment of the indictment to downgrade the responsibility and crime base alleged against these two accused to make the case more suitable for referral under Rule 11 bis?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was indeed not at all the purpose. The purpose was in response to a Rule 72 motion by an accused in the case by Sredoje Lukic to give greater detail and specificity to existing allegations which with we think, having looked at the original indictment, was very much in order; to clarify the temporal and territorial extent of the indictment; to give greater specificity to the modes of liability alleged; and to replace allegations of violence to life and person with allegations of cruel treatment. It was to actually implement better pleading practices. Whether there may be also -- I'm sure both Chambers, both the Referral Bench and any Trial Chamber, would also look to a well-pled indictment as a fundamental tool to know where to go with a case in terms of assessments of trial time, et cetera, et cetera. But it was certainly not any type of page-by-page conformity. However, if it were, which it was not, but if it were, it would not bar consideration by this Chamber because the appropriate underlying reasons were based on a Rule 72 motion. In fact, looking at the evidence, irrespective of where the case is tried, it should be tried so that it is not a long case, concisely, with adequate notice to the accused as to what the charges are, and to remove things that, in the interests of evidence in time, would not be necessary to go forward on. So, no, Your Honours, there was not the concern or the overlap, as one says. But had there been, we submit it would only have been good practice in pleading. We reminded constantly -- we are reminded by the Chambers we must engage in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions. First of all, a question for the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has been argued by one of the defendants that the recent OSCE reports in Jankovic and Stankovic would make it appropriate for the -- for Bosnia-Herzegovina to respond to the criticism. As they said: "It's incumbent upon the Referral Bench to seek supplemental current submissions from the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the concerns raised in the OSCE reports in Jankovic and Stankovic." I'm not asking to you to respond right away, but would you consider, after having read the concerns by the defendant -- by counsel for Milan Lukic to respond to those concerns and submit, on short notice, your response to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best to provide a response to your question. Should my question be incomplete -- should my answer be incomplete, I would like to ask the Chamber to set a deadline in the near future for us to provide a written response. Looking at the law on referral of cases, and comparing it or analysing it in light of the concerns contained in the OSCE report, I would like to say that Articles 2(1) and 1(2) on the law on referral make it clear that the basic principle applied here is the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina in all cases, except when the law on referral stipulates that the law on the criminal procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina are not going to be applied. However, different approaches were used in the two cases that were initially referred, Jankovic and Stankovic, in the light of the complexity of the referral procedure itself. The referral of the cases is a new phenomena on the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was to be expected that the situations which had appeared earlier were not fully foreseeable and not the application of the law itself. Some lack of clarity in interpretation of the law when applied to a specific situation has now been resolved in the Meakic case, where the Court took a different decision when taking into account the requirements for detention as they existed prior to the referral and comparing them to the current provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The law on referral, Article 2.4, stipulates that the detention is to be ruled upon in accordance with the procedures -- provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thus, it is clear that there is sufficient legal guarantees in existence now. As for certain shortcomings that existed in the initial few cases, that is not to be seen as something that will continuously be present in our practice. There are certain amendments in the law on referral, Article 8 and some other articles, which provide for an urgent procedure in transferring documents and files. Thus, the criticism contained in the OSCE report was taken into account by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina which, as a result of that, now anticipates certain amendments to the law. There was a decision of the Appeals Chamber of the ICTY in the case against Mitar Rasovic and Todovic. The decision was dated the 4th of September, 2006. On page 39 of that decision, the Appeals Chamber stated that, despite certain errors committed by the Chambers in previous cases when it came to applying relevant provisions, the Referral Chamber did not overstep its discretion when it found that there is sufficient legal -- that there is sufficient legal framework in existence in Bosnia-Herzegovina to guarantee that all of the rights of the accused will be upheld. In addition to that, I would like to quote from another decision of the ICTY Appeals Chamber, of the 4th September 2006, once again, the case against Rasovic and Todovic. There, in the decision, under paragraph 124, the Chamber stated that: "The Referral Chamber did not err when it granted the referral motion by finding that all of the requirements for a fair trial were met." If the Chamber is not satisfied with the response provided right now, I would kindly like to ask you to allow us to submit further written submissions on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Popadic. I have a question for you, Ambassador Obradovic. You referred to the sentence imposed 20 years in absentia. Is that an enforceable sentence, or should the accused -- should the convicted and sentenced person be retried if he arrives in the Republic of Serbia? In some systems, a trial in absentia should be replaced by a -- a judgement in absentia should be replaced by a judgement as a result of a trial in the presence of the accused. Systems are different. I'd like to know: What's the situation in Serbia? But I do see that you are perhaps looking to Mr. Knezevic, if he could briefly answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will provide a brief answer to that question, Your Honour. When a person was convicted in absentia, as soon as the conditions exist for him to be tried in his presence, there will be a retrial and that person will be tried in his presence. But all of the evidence adduced so far in the previous proceedings would be taken into account, as is stipulated in the law on the competence of state organs in war crimes trials. And this is in accordance with Article 18 of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Serbia, and also the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY would be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knezevic. Mr. Dieckmann, I have two short questions to you. You have very much -- well, first of all, you introduced what you said as a fair trial issue, whereas I now understand that you find that it's a violation of human rights, not necessarily of a fair trial issue. If you refer to the European Convention on Human Rights, I would find fair trial guarantees in Article 6, whereas the nulla poena principle is found in Article 7 is not directly linked to fair trial issues. First of all, is that a fair understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the point we wanted to make is we have to take a look for the concrete situation of the accused in a trial situation and the system governing it. And so you have understood me right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it might be that they had a fair trial but a wrong decision was taken because the decision was inconsistent with the European Convention on Human Rights Article 7 and the lex mitior principle. May I then ask you, since you so much emphasised the lex mitior principle, as you know, the Referral Bench has left it open what law to apply. Would it mean that the charges - of course if proven - brought against Sredoje Lukic would be covered by other legislation, the legislation, perhaps, which was in force at the time? Would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Due to our point of view, the alleged crimes against Mr. Sredoje Lukic is covered under Article 142 of the former Criminal Code of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would that bring a lighter or a heavier maximum penalty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Due to our point of view, it is a substantial difference if you have a Criminal Code to be applied with a maximum penalty of 20 years or if you have a Criminal Code which opens the door for criminal punishment over 20 years or up to lifetime imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So if you evaluate the level of penalty, of course, it will be the more lenient penalty if have you a maximum of 20 years, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time capital punishment - of course it could not be applied - was the maximum penalties for 142?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is our point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then another question: What -- you gave a few examples. Was any of these sentences imposed above the maximum that would be applicable under the law you think should have been applied?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This is a difficult question, Your Honour, because of course these decisions we have quoted have been made in a different law system, with a different maximum of penalty. And so I think it's difficult to compare. But I think if we impose Article 142, it must be a smaller penalty than is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the question is quite simple to answer. The answer is no. But you want to draw our attention to the fact that in the context of maximum penalties, that the actual penalty imposed should have fit within that other context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's well understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I have one question for the Ambassador of Argentina. Argument very much relied upon rules of extradition, the Argentinian law on extradition. Do you consider referral to Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, or to Serbia, extradition, or would you consider it not exactly extradition? Because just -- I'm sure you are aware of that, that if a case is referred, the Tribunal does not require any previous warrant of arrest, which is usual for extraditions, and the Tribunal keeps an eye, to say, on the proceedings and could take proceedings back if there's reason to do so. So to that extent, referrals are considered by this Referral Bench not to be the same as extradition, and the Referral Bench has considered in that context as well that where states are free to engage in extradition relations and are free to formulate, to legislate their conditions, that -- the duty to cooperate with the Tribunal is, well, to say it briefly, is an unconditional one. To what extent have you considered these specific aspects when you formulated today the position of the Government of Argentina?

utterances.speaker: MR. GONI
utterances.text: I understand your question clearly, Your Honour. I am nonetheless constrained by my instructions and have not taken part in drawing them up. As Ambassador in Holland, I have received instructions directly from Buenos Aires. I would, though, be more than happy to take your question from the record, if you allow, and put it to the authorities in Argentina, if you feel that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are invited to do so. Judge Kwon has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have just one matter to ask about the position of the representative of Bosnia, whether it can be answered by Ms. Popadic or Mr. Strika. You must have noted from the submission of Ms. Somers that the amendment -- the indictment against these two accused has been cut down in terms of forms of responsibility, as well as crime base. My question is whether you see a possibility that the -- those charges cut down by the Prosecutor would be added again to the indictment when referred.

utterances.speaker: MS. POPADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will tell you what the positive legislation is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course the answer to your question follows: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are legal preconditions enabling the amendment of an indictment, adding on the new counts if new information about the facts becomes available. This can also be done after the proceedings become final. New proceedings can be instituted for actions or facts not covered by the previous trial. The positive legislation places no limit on this possibility. The application of law applies to proceedings conducted both before domestic judicial organs as well as other proceedings, including those referred by the Tribunal. The authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina consider that in this particular case, the Bench will issue a decision based on the indictment which is being considered here, not based on assumptions that the judicial organs will acquire new facts or new evidence which would enable the indictment to be amended with new counts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions. I've kept a record of who has still some time remaining. Perhaps, Ms. Somers, you first. How much time do you think you would need? I take part of your answer to add to the answers to Judge Kwon as you add to your argument. If you would like to add something, we'll give you a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I kept that one to Judge Kwon very, very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions: One at the beginning and one at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to avail myself of comment and observation. First of all, further to the Benches affirmation above its rulings that 11 bis proceedings do not constitute extradition, affirmed by the Appeals Chamber, we would like to firmly place our position that no condition, no condition, can be put on any action of this Chamber by a member country, responding under Article 29, through its Chapter 7 obligations, as to how business is done with respect to referral or not. The issue is the country's obligation to this Tribunal as an organ of the United Nations Security Council. I was concerned that perhaps the record did not reflect that there was correspondence to the Government of Argentina about the existence of 11 bis proceedings. I would like to just -- so that perhaps the Registry file can be checked, put out to Your Honours, correspondence dated 1st -- 2nd December, 2005, addressed to the embassy of Argentina in The Hague, responding to issues whether the Tribunal has resolved their request for referral in the case raised by the Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte. The Referral Bench -- the Referral Bench has not resumed on the request. "On 1 December 2005, the Prosecutor filed a motion before the Referral Bench to suspend consideration of the request until Milan Lukic is delivered to The Hague. The Office of the Prosecutor would highly appreciate the embassy of Argentina transmitting this information to the appropriate authorities." Secondly, there is correspondence from 16 December 2005 to the embassy of Argentina in The Hague. "On 15 December, the Referral Bench of the International Tribunal decided to suspend consideration of the request of the Prosecutor to refer the indictment against Milan Lukic to Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence until Milan Lukic has been transferred to the seat of the Tribunal in The Hague. "The decision of 14 December 2005 and the decision of 15 December 2005 are attached hereto." Further, the Republic of Argentina has, and I read from its translation of course only, acknowledged, again indicating that extradition is not a consideration, but has acknowledged nonetheless the very strong and definitive wording of Rules of Procedure and Evidence 58 which should there have been an issue, which there was not, of extradition, the obligations laid down in Article 29 of the Statute shall prevail over any legal impediment to the surrender or transfer of the accused or of a witness to the Tribunal which may exist under the national law or extradition treaties of the state concerned. The reference to Rule 58 is contained in correspondence which is part of the Registry file, as I understand, dated 10 January 2006. Certainly copies can be provided easily to the Bench should it not be readily available -- should they not be readily available to the -- through Registry. Further, there is the acknowledgement that -- I'll take just a moment, because I think the quote is significant: "Therefore, let us remember that Rule 58 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal stipulates that the obligations laid down in Article 29 of the Statute prevails over." Quote from the letter. Any attempt with respect to opposed conditions or limitations on the powers that are vested in this Tribunal would simply be of no force. In fact, any country, whether it be Argentina or Brazil or whatever, stands in the same shoes with respect to Article 29 as any republic of the former Yugoslavia in terms of obligations to cooperate with, surrender -- or transfer, rather, use the term "transfer," of an indictee to The Hague. Even provisions for -- for notifying the Security Council in the absence of cooperation, as is required, exist in our Rules. So I just want to make it very clear that the Prosecution's position rests firmly in the decisional law of this Tribunal which is reasoned and based on a full exploration of the reasoning behind the process of referral. Moving on to comments by Serbia, this Chamber, affirmed by the Appeals Chamber -- this Bench, excuse me, affirmed by the Appeals Chamber, has employed the test of greater nexus as opposed to any strict hierarchial selection for the venue in which a case may be tried on transfer. The points of nexus in this case are the victims, who principally reside in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the crimes were committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the well-documented ability and readiness of the Bosnia courts to handle such cases. Serbia, by virtue only of a possible link through citizenship, does not stand up in this particular interest -- in this particular instance to the test that has been principally employed by this Referral Bench. There is nothing -- perhaps in contradiction to my learned counsel opposite to Mr. Yatvin has suggested, unique about this case with respect to referral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it unique that a case still has to be retried and therefore the situation of the exercise of jurisdiction might be a new element which we have not seen before?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In terms of referral, Your Honour. Are we not talking about referral? I beg your pardon. Perhaps I didn't make the transition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just generally -- again, Serbia would not have been a country of designation by the Office of the Prosecutor, and as I observed at the beginning of these proceedings, it was not a country of designation proprio motu by this Bench. Indeed, the equities for trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina are strong. In terms of the uniqueness of the indictment, I need not really remind the Bench, which well knows that the Omarska camp, which was described as a joint criminal enterprise in and of itself, reflecting some of the worst horrors on the continent of Europe since the Second World War, nonetheless had its commander referred to Bosnia-Herzegovina for trial in a national court, and that in fact all the circumstances strongly support referral both on gravity and level of both of the accused. And they should be tried together in a national court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, adding up the time at the beginning and the time you took now ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I cannot -- I will not be able to respond to my learned counsel opposite, Mr. Dieckmann's comments, in the interest of time, but I think the Chamber has asked many of the questions necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Yatvin, you still have some time in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that the Court really captured it, Your Honour, when you said "not exactly extradition". That's the problem; that we have the transfer to the Tribunal, which is not an extradition because the United Nations has decided that its member nations, in order to allow this Tribunal to do its job, must transfer people to the Tribunal, and that is not exactly an -- that is not an extradition, that is something different. It is somehow a horse of a different colour. But the re-transfer by the Tribunal to another nation, I submit that if it walks like a duck, if it quacks like a duck, if it has feathers like a duck, it's probably a duck. That's what we have here. We have what is essentially an extradition from the Tribunal to the nation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that no verbal prestidigitation will get us away with that. That's what we're dealing with. That's why I submit that the Prosecutor's reference to Rule 58 is ill-taken, because Rule 58 clearly talks about conditions of transfer to the Tribunal. To the Tribunal. It doesn't say anything about transfer away from the Tribunal. And the government -- the sovereign nation of Argentina had very good reasons to ensure that the mechanism would not be used as a pass-through, as a ruse, to avoid having the opportunity to ensure that its laws are abided with, that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina should come to Argentina to petition it. If they want Mr. Lukic there, and they didn't even ask, they're relying on this Referral Bench to do its dirty work, and I think that's inappropriate. And I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have to object to the characteristic and ask that either it be stricken from the record or counsel cease from that type of characterisation. The Prosecutor's actions -- there is no basis, it is offensive, and not part of this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Actually, it was describing -- I said the government of Bosnia, not the Prosecutor. But I will withdraw the term, Your Honour. It does not carry the pejorative in my lexicon that I think the Prosecutor assumes, but I apologise, and I mean no disrespect to the nation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But perhaps it would be more appropriate to say "carry water" for that nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the last words of Mr. Yatvin, it will stay in the record and the Chamber has taken notice of what you said, Mr. Yatvin, what you first said and what you then said.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: I'm not going to say any more on that topic. I think the Bench is quite clear on our position. I do -- I did omit one thing when I was talking about Ms. Somers' assertion that she would stand firm live -- the Prosecution would stand firmly on their submissions. I forgot one other submission. The Prosecutor's request at paragraph 10, the original request to transfer, quotes from the President of the Security Council's statement which, as this Bench knows, is something that the Security Council resolutions and 11 bis have incorporated. And one of the categories of persons that it talks about not to be transferred, it mentions paramilitary leaders. And I have argued that in my submission, but the additional point I wanted to make about the paramilitary leaders is we must assume it's -- it's a fundamental tenant of statutory construction, that we must assume that the words mean something, that they had an intent. And as I understand it, there have been no other pure paramilitary leaders since these remarks were made before the Tribunal. Mr. Lukic is it. There are people who were police, who may have had some connection with paramilitary, and there are politicians who may have incited paramilitary, but from my canvassing of the indictments before this Tribunal - and obviously there are a lot and they are lengthy - but there are no other paramilitary leaders. So if you say that because Mr. Lukic is only a paramilitary leader, confined to a certain geographic venue and a certain temporal venue, even relying on the indictment, which I certainly don't think you should, he's not appropriate for transfer because he fits exactly into that definition, and you can't say, Well, there are other paramilitary leaders who are more appropriate for the Tribunal because there are no others that I can see that have been charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Somebody who died.

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, somebody who died in 1998, before the Security Council President made his remarks and before the Security Council resolutions in 2002/2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else, Mr. Yatvin?

utterances.speaker: MR. YATVIN
utterances.text: No, unless the Bench had any other questions for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't have any other questions for you, nor do any of my colleagues. We are close where we have to finish if it were only for the technical reasons of a tape.
